planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Pinkie, introduced in 1928, is a compact polyantha whose main claim to fame today is the much larger climbing sport discovered on it in 1952.

directions: Pinkie forms a low, dense, well-mannered polyantha shrub that produces large clusters of small, semi-double, clear rose-pink flowers in a heavy spring flush with lighter repeat bloom through summer and fall. It tolerates poor soil, humidity, and some shade better than most roses and needs little spraying to stay healthy in the Deep South. Deadhead spent clusters to tidy the plant and encourage continued bloom, and prune lightly in late winter to maintain its compact, rounded shape.

planting.note: Set out own-root or grafted plants in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; America, the 1976 All-America Rose Selections winner, is best known today for the taller climbing sport it later produced.

directions: America bears warm coral-orange to salmon-pink, high-centered, hybrid-tea-shaped blooms with a rich, spicy fragrance on a vigorous, upright grandiflora shrub. It repeat-blooms through the growing season from late spring into fall, holding up well to heat once established. Deadhead spent blooms to sustain the flowering cycle, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new growth and flower production.

common_name: Bitsy Green Hosta (Narrow-Leaved Miniature Green Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Bitsy Green is a Savory's Gardens miniature grown as the green-leaved companion to the gold-leaved sport Bitsy Gold.

directions: Bitsy Green forms a low, tidy mound of narrow, slightly wavy, elliptic green leaves on a slow-growing, long-lived miniature clump, lacking the gold coloring of its sport Bitsy Gold but matching it in scale and habit. Pale lavender flowers rise on short scapes in summer above the dense foliage. Its small mature size makes it well suited to troughs, rock gardens, and the front of a small-scale shaded planting, and it pairs attractively with its gold-leaved counterpart for a two-tone edging effect. Divide congested clumps only occasionally, since it increases slowly, and watch for slugs on tender new growth.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Floradale is a 1965-registered Darwin hybrid tulip best known today as the parent of the ivory-white sport Ivory Floradale.

directions: Floradale produces large, clear golden-yellow blooms on sturdy, wind-resistant stems typical of the Darwin hybrid class, opening in mid-spring well after the earliest species tulips. Like other Darwin hybrids it perennializes better than most tulip types where winters provide adequate chilling, though in mild-winter Southern gardens it is usually most reliable treated as a fresh fall planting. Deadhead after bloom and allow the foliage to yellow and die back completely before removing it, so the bulb can store energy for the following season.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in well-drained soil; Hollywood is a mid-century viridiflora tulip grown today chiefly as the parent of the variegated-leaf sport Esperanto.

directions: Hollywood bears deep scarlet-red flowers with a broad central green flame running up each petal, the defining feature of the viridiflora class, opening late in the tulip season on plain green foliage. Its vivid, two-tone coloring makes a bold accent toward the back of a bulb bed or border. As with most tulips, mild-winter Southern gardens get the best results treating it as a fresh fall bulb planting rather than counting on it to reliably perennialize. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom before removing it.

common_name: Santa Barbara Bearded Iris (Historic Mid-Century Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Santa Barbara is a mid-20th-century tall bearded iris grown today mainly for its role in the pedigree of later award-winning blue and white cultivars.

directions: Santa Barbara carries clear blue-violet Tall Bearded flowers of good midcentury form and substance on well-branched stems. Its lasting significance is as a breeding parent: Eva Faught used it in the complex cross that produced the pale blue 'Cahokia' and its darker sibling 'Pierre Menard', and Paul Cook later crossed it with 'Castalia' and then 'Great Lakes' to breed the silvery light blue 'Distance', an early ancestor behind decades of later dark blue Dykes Medal winners. Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed in sharply drained soil, since standing moisture around the rhizome quickly causes rot. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: Santa Clara Bearded Iris (Historic Mid-Century Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Santa Clara is a mid-20th-century tall bearded iris documented today chiefly through its place in the pedigree of the pale blue 'Cahokia'.

directions: Santa Clara is a Tall Bearded iris of midcentury American breeding whose own flower form is less documented today than its significance as a breeding parent. Along with 'Purissima' and 'Santa Barbara', it stood behind Eva Faught's complex seedling cross that produced the historically important pale blue 'Cahokia', registered in 1948, which itself went on to parent later Dykes Medal winners including 'Whole Cloth' and 'Babbling Brook'. Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Oriflamme is an 1875 French amoena-type bearded iris grown today mainly by historic-iris collectors and as an ancestor of later fragrant tall bearded cultivars.

directions: Oriflamme is a nineteenth-century French amoena bearded iris with pale lavender-white standards over richer violet-purple falls, an antique color pattern that made it an influential parent in early American and European iris breeding. It stands behind the lineage of the 1933 Williamson introduction 'Castalia', a strongly fragrant tall bearded iris described as descended from it. Grow it exactly as other historic bearded iris: full sun and sharply drained soil, with rhizomes set shallowly and the top surface exposed so standing moisture cannot collect around the crown. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Alicia Clare Louisiana Iris (Breeding Line Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Alicia Clare is a Louisiana iris cultivar known today chiefly through its use as a breeding parent in Heather Pryor's Tasmanian hybridizing program.

directions: Alicia Clare is a Louisiana iris cultivar whose principal garden-history significance is as a parent: Australian hybridizer Heather Pryor crossed it with a sibling seedling to breed the heavily ruffled, deep blue-violet 'Swirling Waters', registered in 2001. Its own flowers follow the typical broad-petaled, flat-faced Louisiana iris form, growing from spreading rhizomes that thrive in constantly wet soil. Grow it in full sun with rich, consistently moist to wet soil along a pond margin, ditch bank, or rain garden, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer to maintain vigorous bloom.
